clue.text: Dance curtailed by proper royal residence

indicators.note: to curtail is to cut short, and here a word is cut short by losing its tail, its final letter

parts.note: a ball is a formal dance; it loses its last letter
proper in the sense of decent, upright

explanation.surface: A dance is cut short by the strict etiquette of a royal household.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' simply places the two pieces side by side. BALMORAL is the British royal family's castle in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Balmoral Castle in Aberdeenshire is a private Scottish home of the British monarch, an example of the category.

clue.text: Transport tons in chest

parts.note: a bus is a means of public transport
T is the standard abbreviation for tons

explanation.surface: Heavy goods are carried inside a large box or trunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chest' looks like a storage box, but it is the body part; 'in' only joins the wordplay to that definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A bust is a person's upper torso, especially a woman's breasts, so it is a synonym for the body's front.

clue.text: Three learners welcoming university's reduction in activity

indicators.note: to welcome someone is to take them in, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: L is learner, as on a learner driver's plate, taken three times
U is the usual abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: Three student drivers being taken on by a university makes for a quiet spell.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is read as 'is', joining the wordplay to the definition. The U goes in after the first of the three Ls.
explanation.definitionFit: A lull is a temporary quiet period, a pause or slackening when things go calm for a while.

clue.text: Dismissed from lesson, could one say, nothing like as good as the others?

definitions.meaning: whimsical first meaning: put out of the class, like a pupil sent from the room

definitions.text: nothing like as good as the others
definitions.meaning: second meaning: comprehensively beaten or surpassed by rivals

explanation.surface: A pupil sent out of class is, the clue wonders, simply not up to the standard of classmates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Could one say' admits the first meaning is a playful literal reading: OUT of CLASS, plus a verb ending. The second is the real dictionary sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To be outclassed is to be far surpassed by superior competitors, clearly inferior in skill or quality.

clue.text: From the heights of Peru, a new cathedral head

parts.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new
a dean is the senior cleric in charge of a cathedral

explanation.surface: A newly appointed head of a cathedral arrives from high in the mountains of Peru.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cathedral head' tempts you to take the first letter of cathedral; it is a whole person, the DEAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Andean describes things belonging to the Andes, the mountain range running through Peru, so it fits a highland origin.

clue.text: Grand decay producing rubbish

parts.note: G is short for grand, slang for a thousand
rot is decay

explanation.surface: A once-grand building falls into decay and becomes junk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grand' looks like an adjective but is the noun for a thousand pounds or dollars, abbreviated G. GROT is British slang for junk or filth.
explanation.definitionFit: Grot is informal British slang for worthless, dirty stuff, a colloquial synonym for junk or trash.

clue.text: Counter-bid from rebel duo failing

indicators.note: something failing falls apart, so these letters collapse and are rebuilt in another order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pair of insurgents, their uprising collapsing, make a defiant counter-offer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Counter-bid' sounds like haggling, but it is a term from the card game bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: In bridge, a redouble is the call made after an opponent doubles, raising the stakes again in reply.

clue.text: Regular occurrences of dust easy to transform

indicators.note: to transform something is to change its form, so the letters take a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Dust settles regularly and is easily changed into something else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regular occurrences' is deliberately vague: these are days of the week, recurring every seven days.
explanation.definitionFit: Each weekday comes round on a fixed weekly cycle, so the days themselves are things that happen at set intervals.

clue.text: Being alone outside, wandering around lake

indicators.note: to be around something is to surround it, so one piece is wrapped about another
something wandering strays from its path, so the letters drift out of order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A lone walker strolls outdoors, rambling round a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside' looks like a position word but is the anagram fodder; its scrambled letters wrap round the L for lake.
explanation.definitionFit: Solitude is the state of being on one's own, without company, so it equals the gerund phrase.

clue.text: Boundary shrubs trimmed at front and side

indicators.note: trimming cuts something back, and doing it at the front takes off the opening letter

parts.note: a hedge is a row of shrubs marking a boundary; its first letter goes

explanation.surface: A garden hedge on the property line is clipped along its front and its side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boundary' wants to be the definition, but it belongs to the wordplay, describing a HEDGE; the definition is the last word, 'side'.
explanation.definitionFit: An edge is the outer border or flank of something, so it is a synonym for a side, as of a table.

clue.text: Is one's playing career on the slide?

definitions.text: Is one's playing career on the slide?

parts.note: surface reading: a sportsman whose career is in decline
setter's reading: a musician whose playing is done by moving a sliding tube

explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing career' and 'on the slide' suggest a fading athlete; the question mark flags that the slide is literal, the moving part of a brass instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: A trombone is pitched by pushing a U-shaped slide in and out, so its player's whole performance depends on that mechanism.

clue.text: Obvious some applause means faultless performance

parts.note: clear means obvious, plain to see
a round of applause is a burst of clapping

explanation.surface: Clearly, a burst of clapping signals a flawless show.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition comes from show jumping, where the term is everyday language for a horse and rider with no faults.
explanation.definitionFit: In show jumping a clear round is a course completed without knocking down fences or refusing, so with zero penalties.

clue.text: Mused about pool before first of dives

parts.note: a pond is a small pool of water
ere is an old word for before

indicators.note: the first of anything is its opening item, so only the leading letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of dives

explanation.surface: Someone stands at the pool's edge, deep in thought before the first dive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' looks like it only orders the pieces, but it supplies letters itself: ERE, the poetic word for before.
explanation.definitionFit: To ponder something is to think it over carefully, so pondered means considered or reflected on it.

clue.text: Possible to interpret assortment of bread and ale

indicators.note: an assortment is a mixed selection, so the letters come out jumbled together

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pub's mixed offering of bread and beer is open to interpretation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And' here just joins the two words of anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing that is readable can be deciphered or made sense of, which is what being interpretable means.

clue.text: Old, crowded Danish city

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old
dense means packed closely together

explanation.surface: An ancient, packed city in Denmark.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a description of the city, but the two adjectives are the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Odense, on the island of Funen, is Denmark's third-largest city and the birthplace of Hans Christian Andersen.

clue.text: Intelligence chief's name for emoji

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the surname of John le Carré's fictional spymaster
second meaning: a simple yellow grinning face used in messages

explanation.surface: A spy boss gives a codename to a little picture used in texts.
explanation.walkthrough: The spymaster is fictional: George Smiley runs British intelligence in le Carré's Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy and its sequels.
explanation.definitionFit: The fictional spy shares his surname with the round cartoon face that is the standard grinning emoticon.

clue.text: To separate wheat from chaff is instant success?

parts.note: a win is a success
now means at this instant, immediately

explanation.surface: Is sorting grain from husks a quick victory?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the whimsy: an instant success is a win right now, so the pieces read in reverse of the clue's word order.
explanation.definitionFit: Winnowing blows air through threshed grain so the light husks fly off, the farming method of sorting good from waste.

clue.text: Was a Spice Girl performing nothing on this instrument?

parts.note: to 'do' a celebrity is to impersonate them; Geri Halliwell was Ginger Spice
to do is to perform
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A Spice Girl stands on stage with an instrument but plays nothing on it.
explanation.walkthrough: The Spice Girls were a 1990s British pop group; Geri Halliwell was one of them, so playing her is DID GERI.
explanation.definitionFit: The didgeridoo is a long wooden wind tube of Aboriginal Australian origin, blown to produce a deep drone.

clue.text: Heavy blow for party

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a political setback for a party; in fact the two phrases are separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a forceful hit and informal slang for a lively social gathering or celebration.

clue.text: Somewhat safer nutrient for plant not flowering

indicators.note: somewhat means to some extent, so only part of the following words is taken

parts.note: the letters run across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A gentler fertiliser is wanted for a plant that refuses to bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is fair because ferns reproduce by spores and never flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Ferns are spore-bearing plants with fronds that never produce blossoms, so the description identifies them.

clue.text: Vestment right to go with medal

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right
the OBE, Officer of the Order of the British Empire, is a British honour awarded as a medal

explanation.surface: Proper ceremonial dress is required to accompany a medal at an investiture.
explanation.walkthrough: OBE is a common crossword stand-in for any medal or honour; it is a British award given by the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: A vestment is a ceremonial garment, and a robe is a long loose formal gown of that kind.

clue.text: Very personal hint

definitions.meaning: first meaning, an adjective: private and close
second meaning, a verb: to suggest indirectly

explanation.walkthrough: The two meanings are pronounced differently: the adjective ends like 'it', the verb like 'ate'.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means private and closely familiar; as a verb it means to imply something without stating it.

clue.text: Depicted Scottish saint, omitting a name

indicators.note: to omit is to leave out, so some letters are dropped from the word

parts.note: St Andrew is the patron saint of Scotland
taken as written; removed
N is the abbreviation for name; removed

explanation.surface: A painting shows Scotland's patron saint, but the artist left off the title.
explanation.walkthrough: The A and N to be dropped happen to sit together at the start of the saint's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Drew is the past tense of draw, and drawing a figure means portraying it, as depicted does.

clue.text: Emotionally arouse boy entertaining sorceress

indicators.note: to entertain a guest is to have them in, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: a son is a boy
a witch is a female sorcerer

explanation.surface: A young lad is thrilled by a visiting enchantress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entertaining' suggests amusement, which suits the surface, but it means holding inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally, to switch someone on is to excite or stimulate their feelings, like flicking on a light.
